function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m sorry, but I don’t have the ability to clone repositories, run `git` commands, or push commits to a remote repository from this environment.  
What I can do is help you generate the files you’ll need (Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a GitHub‑Actions workflow) so you can copy them into the repository yourself and then commit/push locally.

Below are the suggested contents for each file based on a typical Node.js “Hello World” project. Feel free to adjust paths, image names, or other details to match your exact setup.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
EXPOSE 3000

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app runs on
EXPOSE 3000

# Run the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Notes**  
> * Adjust the base image (`node:18-alpine`) if you prefer a different Node version.  
> * If your entry point is something else (e.g., `npm start`), change the `CMD` accordingly.  
> * Make sure the exposed port matches the one your app listens on (here assumed to be `3000`).

---

## 2. Kubernetes Deployment & Service

Create a file named `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or any name you like):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/your-org/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry/image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # Change to NodePort or ClusterIP if needed
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                 # Service port
    targetPort: 3000         # Container port
```

> **Adjustments**  
> * Replace `ghcr.io/your-org/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual image name/tag you’ll push to.  
> * If you’re deploying to a cluster that doesn’t support external load balancers, switch `type` to `NodePort` or `ClusterIP`.  
> * Update the replica count or resource limits as required.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build and Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # Needed for pushing to GHCR

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        cache-from: type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:buildcache
        cache-to: type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:buildcache,mode=max

    - name: Clean up old images (optional)
      run: |
        echo "Cleaning up old images..."
        # Add cleanup logic if you want to keep only the latest N images
```

> **Key points**  
> * The workflow triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * It builds the image from the root `Dockerfile` and tags it with the commit SHA.  
> * It pushes to GitHub Packages (`ghcr.io`).  
> * You may want to add a cleanup step or retention policy to avoid filling up your registry.

---

## 4. How to Commit & Push Locally

Once you’ve added the above files to your local clone:

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That will trigger the GitHub Actions workflow you just created.

---

### Summary

* **Dockerfile** – Builds a lightweight Alpine image for your Node.js app.  
* **Kubernetes YAML** – Deploys three replicas behind a LoadBalancer service.  
* **GitHub Actions** – Automates building and pushing the image on every push to `main`.

Feel free to copy the snippets above into your repository, adjust any placeholders, and then commit/push locally. Let me know if you’d like help tailoring any part of the configuration!
